analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to identify the 20 most toxic-polluted communities and mandate inspections, health studies, and pollution cleanup there.
analysis.headline: The Environmental Justice Act of 1998 never received a hearing or vote; it died in four House committees when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the EPA to publish a list of the 20 counties or areas with the highest toxic chemical levels and resident exposure. In those areas, every covered facility would face mandatory compliance inspections, residents would get grants to hire their own experts, a federal health study would compare disease rates to less-polluted areas, and new toxic facilities could be blocked where pollution was already harming health. It also funded medical screening for pollution-related illness and parks in affected communities.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of the most heavily polluted communities, which are disproportionately low-income and minority neighborhoods. They would get mandated facility inspections, grants to hire independent experts, a federal health study of local disease rates, free medical screening and treatment for pollution-related illnesses, pollution reduction efforts, and park funding.

how_it_helps.text: EPA must publish and regularly update a list of 20 Environmental High Impact Areas where toxic chemical levels and human exposure are highest [S2][S3].
EPA and OSHA must inspect or review every covered toxic chemical facility in those areas within one year of each list's publication [S2][S3].

Residents would receive technical assistance grants to hire independent experts to understand local environmental and health risks, and a federal study would compare health impacts—cancer, birth defects, infant mortality, respiratory disease—in these areas versus elsewhere [S2][S3].

Where pollution is shown to harm health, new toxic facilities could not be sited or permitted unless officials agree there would be no significant health impact, and EPA could take regulatory action if pollution isn't reduced [S2][S3].
Communities with pollution-related illness would get grants for medical screening and treatment for uninsured residents, plus park and green space development funding [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of toxic chemical facilities—chemical plants, hazardous waste sites, and industrial facilities in the designated areas—would bear the cost of mandatory inspections, pollution prevention plans, potential permitting moratoriums, and possible new pollution reduction requirements, including at federal facilities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Toxic chemical facilities in designated areas

drawbacks.text: The bill authorized appropriations of 'such sums as may be necessary' with no cost estimate, so taxpayers would fund the inspections, health studies, grants, and screening programs [S3].

The siting moratorium would let a facility proceed only if the HHS Secretary and EPA Administrator jointly agree there would be no significant adverse health impact, a standard that could delay or block industrial projects in designated areas even where a new facility would be cleaner than existing ones [S3].

A good-faith objection: designating exactly 20 areas by formula risks mislabeling communities, and concentrating enforcement in listed areas could push new facilities to locate just outside the designated boundaries rather than reduce pollution overall [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—inspections of facilities in the most polluted communities, independent expert help for residents, health screening, and pollution reduction—would go to people with the least political power, while the costs fall on facility operators and federal budgets. The moratorium mechanism is blunt and the open-ended funding would need oversight, but the bill's core tradeoff is straightforward: public health spending versus compliance costs for polluting facilities.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-September 1998, weeks before the end of a two-year Congress, and referred to four separate committees; none brought it to a vote before Congress adjourned, so it expired.

narrative.text: Rep. John Lewis introduced the bill on September 16, 1998, with 10 Democratic cosponsors joining [S1][S4][S5].
The Speaker referred it to four committees—Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, and Resources—splitting jurisdiction across panels [S5].
It was sent to four subcommittees between September 23 and September 30, 1998, and no committee or subcommittee acted on it [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill received no hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of toxic chemical facilities in heavily polluted areas were better off, since no mandatory inspections, health studies, or permitting moratoriums took effect. Residents of those communities gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Toxic facility operators; residents gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the Republican-led committees never acted on the bill, and no Republicans are listed in support [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Toxic chemical facilities (chemical plants, hazardous waste handlers, industrial emitters)
industries.note: The bill mandates compliance inspections of every covered facility in designated high-impact areas and can impose a siting moratorium and forced pollution reduction where health harm is found. The industry's cost is the public's health benefit, so its interest runs against residents of polluted communities.

industries.industry: Environmental consulting and public health services
industries.note: New federal grants for resident technical assistance, community medical screening, and pollution reduction strategies would create funded work for independent experts and health providers serving these communities.
